claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a powerful technology to study the ecosystems of normal and disease tissues.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a powerful technology to study the ecosystems of normal and disease tissues.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about scRNA-seq technology.

claim: Gene expression signatures can be used to interrogate single cells for cell identities and other cellular properties using signature-scoring methods.
source: Gene expression signatures can be used to interrogate single cells for cell identities and other cellular properties (Noureen et al., 2021a) using signature-scoring methods.
evidence: Supported by citation to Noureen et al., 2021a.

claim: scRNA-seq data have high dropout rates compared with bulk-sample RNAseq.
source: Compared with bulk-sample RNAseq, scRNA-seq data have high dropout rates (Hicks et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hicks et al., 2018.

claim: Dropout rates are the opposite of gene counts, that is, the number of genes detected in a cell.
source: Dropout rates are the opposite of gene counts, that is, the number of genes detected in a cell, a feature that is associated with cell differentiation status (Gulati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definitional statement with citation support for the association with differentiation status.

claim: Gene counts are associated with cell differentiation status.
source: Dropout rates are the opposite of gene counts, that is, the number of genes detected in a cell, a feature that is associated with cell differentiation status (Gulati et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gulati et al., 2020.

claim: Cancer cells exhibit stem-cell like properties.
source: Cancer cells exhibit stem-cell like properties Malta et al., 2018; thus, cancer may represent such a context.
evidence: Supported by citation to Malta et al., 2018.

claim: The average number of detected genes was significantly higher in tumor cells than in normal cells across all datasets.
source: We found that the average number of detected genes was significantly higher in tumor cells than in normal cells across all datasets (Figure 1A, p < 2.2e-16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p < 2.2e-16) and Figure 1A showing the data.

claim: The imbalance in gene counts between cancer and normal cells persisted when normal cells were separated into different cell populations.
source: This imbalance persisted when we separated normal cells into different cell populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cancer-associated cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF), tumor-associated macrophages (TAM), and tumor-related endothelial cells (TEC) had higher gene counts than other normal cell types.
source: However, cancer-associated cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF), tumor-associated macrophages (TAM), and tumor-related endothelial cells (TEC) had higher gene counts than other normal cell types, sometimes even comparable to malignant cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-cell methods reported similar proportions of up- and down-regulated gene sets (9% vs 12% of all input gene sets).
source: On average, single-cell methods reported similar proportions of up- and down-regulated gene sets (9% vs 12% of all input gene sets) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ssGSEA and GSVA reported 25 and 23% of the input gene sets as upregulated but only 6 and 5% as down regulated.
source: In contrast, ssGSEA and GSVA reported 25 and 23% of the input gene sets as upregulated but only 6 and 5% as down regulated.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: In six out of the 10 datasets, ssGSEA and GSVA estimated more than twice as many upregulated gene sets than down gene sets.
source: In six out of the 10 datasets, ssGSEA and GSVA estimated more than twice as many upregulated gene sets than down gene sets.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: In cell types with high gene counts such as TEC, TAM, and CAF, significantly more upregulated gene sets by ssGSEA and GSVA were not observed.
source: Notably, in cell types with high gene counts such as TEC, TAM, and CAF, we did not observe significantly more upregulated gene sets by ssGSEA and GSVA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: Cohen's d from ssGSEA and GSVA showed consistent positive correlation with gene set sizes.
source: We also found that Cohen's d from ssGSEA and GSVA showed consistent positive correlation with gene set sizes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1C showing correlation data.

claim: Single-cell methods did not demonstrate positive correlation between Cohen's d and gene set sizes.
source: Single-cell methods did not demonstrate this pattern.
evidence: Inferred from the statement following the observation about ssGSEA and GSVA.

claim: GSVA was slower than other methods.
source: We observed that GSVA was slower than other methods.
evidence: Supported by computational performance testing.

claim: Running the head and neck dataset with GSVA using 200 threads on a 2.5 GHz Xeon processor took more than 3 days to complete.
source: For instance, running the head and neck dataset with 200 threads on a 2.5 GHz Xeon processor took more than 3 days to complete.
evidence: Supported by computational performance testing.

claim: GSVA outputs were highly consistent with those of ssGSEA.
source: Because GSVA outputs were highly consistent with those of ssGSEA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and its running speed would not likely scale up to single cell datasets, we dropped GSVA from subsequent analyses.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: All four methods reported a higher score in cycling cells for the cell cycle gene signature (GO:0007049) in the head and neck cancer dataset.
source: We observed all four methods reported a higher score in cycling cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D showing the scores.

claim: ssGSEA scores were significantly higher in non-cycling cancer cells than in normal cells although neither are cycling.
source: However, ssGSEA scores were significantly higher in non-cycling cancer cells than in normal cells although neither are cycling (Student's t test, p < 2.2e-16).
evidence: Supported by statistical test (Student's t test, p < 2.2e-16).

claim: Single-cell-based methods did not show a difference in scores between non-cycling cancer cells and non-cycling normal cells.
source: In contrast, the single-cell-based methods did not show this difference.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with ssGSEA results.

claim: Gene set size had negligible impacts on detection rates.
source: We found gene set size had negligible impacts on detection rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Noise levels had a much bigger impact on detection rates than gene set size.
source: Noise levels, on the other hand, had a much bigger impact.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with gene set size impact.

claim: For up gene sets, all methods were able to detect 50% of the gene sets on average even at the 80% noise level.
source: For up gene sets, all methods were able to detect 50% of the gene sets on average even at the 80% noise level (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2A showing detection rates.

claim: For down gene sets, ssGSEA performed worse than other methods.
source: However, for down gene sets, ssGSEA performed worse than other methods (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2B showing detection rates.

claim: Without noise, ssGSEA only detected about 85% of the down gene sets.
source: Without noise, it only detected about 85% of the gene sets.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: At 80% noise level, ssGSEA detected around 30% of the down gene sets, compared to 70–80% by single-cell methods.
source: At 80% noise level, it detected around 30% of the gene sets, compared to 70–80% by single-cell methods.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: AUCell and JASMINE outperformed SCSE and ssGSEA in specificity.
source: We found AUCell and JASMINE outperformed SCSE and ssGSEA in specificity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2C showing specificity data.

claim: On average, AUCell detected 7.5 and 1.2% of the input gene sets as up and down in the down sampling experiment.
source: On average, AUCell detected 7.5 and 1.2% of the input gene sets as up and down; JASMINE detected 4 and 1%.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: JASMINE detected 4 and 1% of the input gene sets as up and down on average in the down sampling experiment.
source: On average, AUCell detected 7.5 and 1.2% of the input gene sets as up and down; JASMINE detected 4 and 1%.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: In four datasets, SCSE overestimated down regulated gene sets (average 25.4%).
source: In four datasets, SCSE overestimated down regulated gene sets (average 25.4%).
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: ssGSEA grossly overestimated both up- and down regulated gene sets in all datasets (average 11 and 46%, respectively).
source: ssGSEA grossly overestimated both up- and down regulated gene sets in all datasets (average 11 and 46%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: Single-cell methods were robust to down sampling, with little changes in coefficient of variance (CV).
source: We observed that single-cell methods were robust to our down sampling, with little changes in CV.
evidence: Supported by CV analysis in down sampling experiment.

claim: In three datasets, ssGSEA had a higher CV in down-sampled cells than in original cells.
source: However, in three datasets, ssGSEA had a higher CV in down-sampled cells than in original cells.
evidence: Supported by CV analysis in down sampling experiment.

claim: JASMINE aligned better with the consensus in most datasets.
source: JASMINE aligned better with the consensus in most datasets (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: AUCell overall had lower accuracies against the consensus, particularly for down regulated gene sets.
source: AUCell overall had lower accuracies against the consensus, particularly for down regulated gene sets, likely because it is designed to score marker signatures (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2D and includes speculation about the reason.

claim: AUCell showed higher false positive rates when breaking down to sensitivity and specificity.
source: When breaking down to sensitivity and specificity, AUCell showed higher false positive rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The three tools showed comparable sensitivity.
source: The three tools showed comparable sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by data analysis results.

claim: Across the 10 datasets, SCSE and JASMINE showed better correlation.
source: Across the 10 datasets, SCSE and JASMINE showed better correlation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B,C), thus explaining their relatively better alignment with the consensus.
evidence: Supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4B,C.

claim: SCSE was the most efficient computationally.
source: Overall, SCSE was the most efficient computationally.
evidence: Supported by computational efficiency testing.

claim: JASMINE was the second fastest algorithm but required a memory similar to that of ssGSEA.
source: JASMINE was the second fastest algorithm but required a memory similar to that of ssGSEA.
evidence: Supported by computational efficiency testing.

claim: AUCell was slightly faster than ssGSEA but required the most memory.
source: AUCell was slightly faster than ssGSEA but required the most memory.
evidence: Supported by computational efficiency testing.

claim: The computational performances of the methods were robust across signature sizes.
source: Their performances were robust across signature sizes.
evidence: Supported by computational efficiency testing.

claim: As the down sampling rate shifted from low to high, the pattern of deregulated gene sets by ssGSEA also shifted from more up gene sets towards more down gene sets.
source: We observed that as the down sampling rate shifted from low to high, the pattern of deregulated gene sets by ssGSEA also shifted from more up gene sets towards more down gene sets (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observation that ssGSEA scores shift with down sampling rate strongly associates dropouts with ssGSEA scores.
source: This observation strongly associates dropouts with ssGSEA scores.
evidence: Inferred from the down sampling experiment results.

claim: Before entering the dropout zone, the signature score was identical between the no-dropout cell and the 60%-dropout cell in the dummy expression profile simulation.
source: Before entering the dropout zone, the signature score was identical between the no-dropout cell and the 60%-dropout cell.
evidence: Supported by simulation results.

claim: When the floating gene was between ranks 4000 and 7000, the signature was scored higher in the dropout cell than in the no-dropout cell.
source: However, when the floating gene was between ranks 4000 and 7000, the signature was scored higher in the dropout cell; when moving further toward ranks 7000–10,000, the signature was scored lower in the dropout cell.
evidence: Supported by simulation results.

claim: When the floating gene was between ranks 7000 and 10,000, the signature was scored lower in the dropout cell than in the no-dropout cell.
source: However, when the floating gene was between ranks 4000 and 7000, the signature was scored higher in the dropout cell; when moving further toward ranks 7000–10,000, the signature was scored lower in the dropout cell.
evidence: Supported by simulation results.

claim: Dropouts are sufficient to change ssGSEA scores in unintended ways.
source: This simple experiment demonstrates that though tedious, dropouts are sufficient to change ssGSEA scores in unintended ways.
evidence: Inferred from the simulation experiment results.

claim: Single-cell-based methods are more robust at identifying bona fide up- and down regulated gene signatures from scRNAseq data.
source: We show that single-cell-based methods are more robust at identifying bona fide up- and down regulated gene signatures from scRNAseq data.
evidence: Supported by the benchmarking results throughout the study.

claim: Bulk-sample-based ssGSEA and GSVA are more susceptible to dropouts.
source: In contrast, bulk-sample-based ssGSEA and GSVA are more susceptible to dropouts.
evidence: Supported by the benchmarking results throughout the study.

claim: AUCell uses Area Under the Curve (AUC) to test the enrichment of a gene set among top expressed genes in a cell.
source: AUCell uses Area Under the Curve (AUC) to test the enrichment of a gene set among top expressed genes in a cell.
evidence: This is a description of the AUCell method.

claim: SCSE measures a signature using normalized total expression of the signature genes.
source: SCSE measures a signature using normalized total expression of the signature genes.
evidence: This is a description of the SCSE method.

claim: AUCell and SCSE intuitively counter dropout effects by using only expressed genes.
source: AUCell and SCSE intuitively counter dropout effects by using only expressed genes.
evidence: This is an inference about how these methods work.

claim: JASMINE considers the enrichment of signature genes in expressed genes to counter dropout effects, and meanwhile, evaluates the average expression level of the expressed signature genes.
source: JASMINE considers the enrichment of signature genes in expressed genes to counter dropout effects, and meanwhile, evaluates the average expression level of the expressed signature genes.
evidence: This is a description of the JASMINE method.

claim: Bulk-sample-based methods were not designed to deal with excessive dropouts.
source: Bulk-sample-based methods were not designed to deal with excessive dropouts, which may mislead analysis especially if cell biology underpins different dropout rates.
evidence: This is an inference about the design of bulk-sample-based methods.

claim: Among single-cell methods, JASMINE and SCSE showed better concordance.
source: We further show that among single-cell methods, JASMINE and SCSE showed better concordance, and JASMINE outperforms SCSE in down sampling tests.
evidence: Supported by the benchmarking results.

claim: JASMINE outperforms SCSE in down sampling tests.
source: We further show that among single-cell methods, JASMINE and SCSE showed better concordance, and JASMINE outperforms SCSE in down sampling tests.
evidence: Supported by the benchmarking results.

claim: Dropouts were initially thought to result from low amounts of input RNA and transcriptional stochasticity.
source: Dropouts were initially thought to result from low amounts of input RNA and transcriptional stochasticity.
evidence: This is a statement about historical understanding of dropouts.

claim: More studies showed that dropouts are associated with cell states and identities.
source: However, more studies showed that dropouts are associated with cell states and identities (Gulati et al., 2020; Qiu, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gulati et al., 2020 and Qiu, 2020.

claim: In cellular contexts where cells may have systematic differences in dropout rates, any tool that fails to account for dropouts may generate misleading even erroneous data.
source: Thus, in cellular contexts where cells may have systematic differences in dropout rates, any tool that fails to account for dropouts may generate misleading even erroneous data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study results.

claim: It is important to consider cellular contexts when benchmarking methods for scRNA-seq data analysis, particularly when bulk-sample-based methods are involved.
source: Our study also suggests that it is important to consider cellular contexts when benchmarking methods for scRNA-seq data analysis, particularly when bulk-sample-based methods are involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: Gene counts of single cells are associated with cell differentiation status and cell identity.
source: Several recent studies showed that gene counts of single cells are associated with cell differentiation status and cell identity (Gulati et al., 2020; Qiu, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gulati et al., 2020 and Qiu, 2020.

claim: Cells higher in the differentiation hierarchy express more genes.
source: Specifically, cells higher in the differentiation hierarchy express more genes.
evidence: This is a statement based on cited studies.

claim: The study collected 10 scRNA-seq datasets across different cancer types, technological platforms and sequencing coverage.
source: To examine if cancer and normal cells demonstrate similar imbalances, we collected 10 scRNA-seq datasets across different cancer types, technological platforms and sequencing coverage (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: Cell type annotations were obtained from the original studies.
source: We also obtained cell type annotations from the original studies.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study assembled 7503 gene sets from MSigDB that each has at least 20 genes.
source: We assembled 7503 gene sets from MSigDB that each has at least 20 genes (The term 'gene set' is used interchangeably with 'gene signature'; Methods).
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: Cohen's d greater than one was defined as upregulated, and less than –1 as down regulated.
source: For simplicity, we defined Cohen's d greater than one as upregulated, and less than –1 as down regulated.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study used regularized negative binomial regression implemented in Seurat for normalization.
source: We filtered all the data sets by removing non-expressed genes and then applied regularized negative binomial regression implemented in Seurat for normalization.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study used C2 (n = 6226), C3 (n = 3556) and Hallmarks (n = 50) modules from MSigDB v.7.2.
source: We used C2 (n = 6226), C3 (n = 3556) and Hallmarks (n = 50) modules from MSigDB (Subramanian et al., 2005) v.7.2, to calculate the ratio of signature genes across all data sets and further signature scoring.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study used MAST to identify differentially expressed genes for each dataset.
source: We first identified differentially expressed genes for each dataset using MAST (Finak et al., 2015), a method that explicitly accounts for dropout rates.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: MAST is a method that explicitly accounts for dropout rates.
source: We first identified differentially expressed genes for each dataset using MAST (Finak et al., 2015), a method that explicitly accounts for dropout rates.
evidence: This is a description of the MAST method with citation support.

claim: For each signature, JASMINE calculates the approximate mean using gene ranks among expressed genes and the enrichment of the signature in expressed genes.
source: For each signature, JASMINE calculates the approximate mean using gene ranks among expressed genes and the enrichment of the signature in expressed genes.
evidence: This is a description of the JASMINE method.

claim: The two components (mean and enrichment) are then scaled to 0–1 and averaged to result in the final JASMINE score.
source: The two are then scaled to 0–1 and averaged to result in the final JASMINE score.
evidence: This is a description of the JASMINE method.

claim: The mean rank calculation in JASMINE is robust to scale normalization methods.
source: Because the mean is based on ranks, it is robust to scale normalization methods.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the JASMINE method.

claim: JASMINE assesses the expression level of the signature only using genes detected in one cell, thus minimizing the effect of dropouts.
source: It assesses the expression level of the signature only using genes detected in one cell, thus minimizing the effect of dropouts.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the JASMINE method.
